notes.meaning: Abijam took the throne in Judah while Jeroboam was still ruling over the northern tribes. He reigned for about three years in Jerusalem, and his mother Maacah was a descendant of David's son Absalom. His short rule showed that wickedness often cuts a leader's time short.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the author of Kings calls him Abijam rather than Abijah to swap God's name for that of a Canaanite sea god, pointing out his divided loyalties.

notes.meaning: Abijam copied the sinful habits and idol worship of his father Rehoboam. His heart was not fully committed to the Lord the way King David's had been. He spoke about God when it helped him in battle, but he lacked true sincerity.

Even though Abijam was unfaithful, God kept a royal descendant on the throne in Jerusalem. A lamp was an everyday picture for keeping a family name and its kingdom alive. God did this to honor His promise to David rather than giving this unworthy king what he deserved.

David was remembered as a king whose whole life generally pleased the Lord. His one terrible moral failure was his sin against Uriah the Hittite, which brought great shame. Yet because David truly repented, God kept His covenant with David's family line.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that the mention of Uriah is absent from important early Greek manuscripts and may have begun as an explanatory note in the margin.

notes.meaning: Border fighting and hostility continued between Judah and Israel throughout these years. Even though full-scale civil war had been forbidden, tension never really ceased. Sin kept God's divided people from enjoying real peace with each other.
Abijam fought actively against Jeroboam during his brief rule, as recorded in Judah's royal annals. When he died, he was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem, and his son Asa took over the throne.

Asa began ruling Judah during Jeroboam's twentieth year and reigned for forty-one years. His grandmother Maacah still held the honored title of queen mother when he started. A long and steady reign was often a sign of God's blessing on a righteous king.

Asa was a good ruler who pleased the Lord by walking in the godly steps of David. He showed deep devotion to the worship of the one true God. His reign brought a much-needed season of spiritual renewal to the land.

Asa cleaned up the country by driving out the male prostitutes who served at pagan shrines. He also cleared away the false idols that his father and grandfather had set up. True renewal begins by actively putting away evil practices.

Asa even removed his grandmother Maacah from her royal post because she had made a disgusting pagan idol. He chopped down the wooden pole and burned it to ashes in the Kidron Valley outside the city. He respected his family, but he honored God above everything else.

Asa did not manage to take down all the local worship shrines across the countryside. Even so, the Lord looked on his sincere devotion and considered his heart fully loyal throughout his life. God accepts sincere and honest faith even when a believer's work remains incomplete.

Asa brought silver, gold, and sacred dishes into the temple of the Lord. These included gifts that his father had pledged from past victories as well as his own offerings. He made sure that things promised to God were faithfully delivered to His house.

Hostilities broke out between King Asa and King Baasha of Israel. Baasha fortified the town of Ramah, just north of Jerusalem, to set up a military blockade. He did this to stop his own people from traveling south to worship the Lord in Judah.

Instead of trusting the Lord, Asa took leftover silver and gold from the temple and palace to bribe King Ben-hadad of Aram. He urged the Syrian king to break his treaty with Baasha and attack Israel. Asa showed weak faith by using sacred treasures to hire a foreign army.

differ.view: Commentators in this tradition highlight that Asa stumbled by treating Baasha's threat as a smaller problem he could solve with human schemes, failing to trust God as he had during earlier crises.

notes.meaning: Ben-hadad accepted the bribe and sent his generals to attack cities in northern Israel near the Sea of Galilee. When Baasha heard that his northern border was falling, he stopped building Ramah and withdrew to his capital at Tirzah.

King Asa drafted all the men of Judah to carry away the timber and stone Baasha had left behind at Ramah. Asa used those very supplies to fortify his own border towns, Geba and Mizpah. His plan worked, but it had relied on human politics rather than faith in God.

Asa built several fortified cities and accomplished many things during his long rule. In his old age, he suffered from a severe disease in his feet. Sadly, in his final years he looked only to human doctors for help instead of turning back to the Lord.

differ.view: Writers in this tradition often view Asa's foot ailment as God's personal discipline for his lack of faith, stressing the need to seek the Lord for divine healing.

notes.meaning: Asa died and was given an honorable burial alongside his royal ancestors in Jerusalem. His son Jehoshaphat took over the throne and continued to lead the nation in godliness.

Nadab son of Jeroboam ruled over the northern kingdom of Israel for only two years. He copied the bad example of his father, keeping up the golden calf worship that had led the nation into sin. He refused to learn from the warnings God had sent his family.

While Nadab and the army were attacking a Philistine city named Gibbethon, an officer named Baasha plotted against him. Baasha murdered the young king and seized the throne during Asa's third year in Judah.

As soon as Baasha became king, he slaughtered every living member of Jeroboam's family to secure his power. This brutal massacre fulfilled the judgment that the prophet Ahijah had foretold against Jeroboam's house. Baasha acted out of selfish ambition, but God used him to judge Jeroboam's terrible idolatry.

The other events of Nadab's short reign were kept in the royal records of Israel. Border conflicts and hostility continued between Asa and Baasha for the rest of their days. Changing kings in the north did nothing to heal the deep divide between the two nations.

Baasha ruled all Israel from the city of Tirzah for twenty-four years. Even though he had wiped out Jeroboam's family for their wickedness, he kept practicing the exact same calf worship. Sin blinded him so completely that he repeated the very evil that destroyed the dynasty before him.
